extraction_text: Sanjaya completed his mission for Dhritarashtra and bid farewell to the Pandava sons.
Sanjaya arrived at Hastinapura and stood at the entrance to the inner apartments, requesting the doorkeeper to announce his return from the Pandava sons to Dhritarashtra.
The doorkeeper informed Dhritarashtra that Sanjaya had returned from the Pandava sons and was at the door seeking an audience.
Dhritarashtra expressed eagerness to see Sanjaya and ordered him to be admitted immediately.
Sanjaya entered the hall guarded by clever and brave Aryas and approached Dhritarashtra, son of Vichitravirya, who was seated on a lion-throne, with folded hands.
Sanjaya paid respects to Dhritarashtra and conveyed Yudhishthira's greetings and well-wishes to Dhritarashtra, his sons, grandsons, friends, ministers, and dependents.
Dhritarashtra inquired about the welfare of Yudhishthira, his sons, ministers, and brothers.

Sanjaya reported that Yudhishthira and his ministers were well, better than Dhritarashtra had imagined, and described Yudhishthira's virtues including adherence to dharma and artha, thoughtfulness, learning, insight, and good conduct.
Sanjaya explained Yudhishthira's principles: humility above dharma, dharma above wealth accumulation, and that Yudhishthira would not abandon dharma for pleasure.
Sanjaya reflected on human actions being controlled by others like puppets by strings, and seeing Yudhishthira in adversity, concluded that karma/destiny is superior to human effort.
Sanjaya criticized Dhritarashtra's evil deeds causing terrible sins, stating that only reasonable desires earn praise.
Sanjaya declared that Yudhishthira had discarded sin like a snake shedding old skin and through steadfast action had won glory, throwing the sin back to Dhritarashtra.
Sanjaya warned Dhritarashtra that his own actions were ignoble,背离 dharma and利益, bringing condemnation in this world and potential sin in the next if he remained inattentive.
Sanjaya accused Dhritarashtra of being controlled by his sons, neglecting others, coveting questionable wealth, and gaining ill repute on earth.
Sanjaya described characteristics leading to disaster: lack of wisdom, low birth, roughness, vengefulness, neglect of Kshatriya learning, lack of courage, and lack of culture.

Sanjaya described the virtuous person: high birth, adherence to dharma, renowned, learned, living pleasantly, self-controlled, fulfilling dual duties of dharma and利益, and bound by fate with no other choice.

attributes.condition: Bound by fate with no choice

extraction_text: The text presents a classification of people into three categories (upper, middle, lower) who should be assigned duties according to regulations.
It states that three types of people should not own property: wives, slaves, and sons, as any property they acquire belongs to their master.
It advises that a wise and powerful king should avoid four types of people: the unintelligent, the procrastinator, the lazy, and the flattering singer, and not consult them on state affairs.
It recommends that in a wealthy household, four types of people should be allowed to live: elderly relatives, high-born people who have fallen on hard times, poor friends, and childless sisters.

It mentions that Brihaspati (Vrihaspati) answered the questions of Indra (Sakra) of the Thirty-Three Gods, speaking of four current matters: the intentions of the gods, the intuition of the wise, the humility of scholars, and the destruction of evildoers.
It instructs that a person should strive to serve the five fires: father, mother, fire (Agni), self, and teacher.
It states that one can only gain reputation in the world by offering to five types of people: gods, ancestors, humans, ascetics, and guests.
It notes that wherever one goes, five types of people follow: friends, enemies, neutrals, dependents, and seekers of refuge.
It uses an analogy that if one of a person's five senses is damaged, wisdom leaks out like water from a hole in a water bag.
It advises that a person aspiring for prosperity should abandon six vices: sleepiness, slackness, fear, anger, laziness, and procrastination.

It advises to abandon six types of people like a leaking boat in the ocean: a teacher who does not teach, a priest who does not study, a king who does not protect, a wife who speaks harshly, a herdsman who desires a village, and a barber who desires a forest.
It advises never to lose six virtues: truthfulness, charity, diligence, non-envy, tolerance, and steadfastness.

It states that six types of people depend on six others for survival: a thief depends on the negligent, a doctor on the sick, a wayward woman on the lustful, a priest on the sacrificer, a king on litigants, and a wise person always on the foolish.

It warns that a king should forever abandon seven vices that bring disaster and can destroy even a well-established king: women, dice, hunting, drinking, harsh speech (fifth), severe punishment, and squandering wealth.

It lists eight precursors to a person's destruction: hating Brahmins, quarreling with Brahmins, taking Brahmin property, attempting to murder Brahmins, liking to blame them, disliking to praise them, not seeking them for matters, and envying their requests.
The text lists eight sources of happiness that bring joy upon sight.
A wise person understands the body as a house with nine gates, three pillars, five witnesses, and governed by the soul.
Ten things contrary to dharma are listed: addiction to alcohol, negligence, arrogance, laziness, anger, hunger and thirst, haste, cowardice, greed, and lust.

attributes.source: Ancient history recited by Asura King Shukra to his son

extraction_text: A king who abandons desire and anger, gives to the deserving, distinguishes right from wrong, is learned, acts swiftly, and serves as a model for people.
A king who knows how to appease subjects, punish the wicked, and exercise moderation and tolerance attracts all prosperity.
A wise person does not despise weak enemies, uses intelligence against enemies, avoids fighting the strong, shows courage at the right time.
A leader who does not grieve in misfortune, remains diligent, perseveres, controls self, and endures suffering will conquer enemies.
A person who avoids wandering blindly, associating with wicked people, touching others' wives, pride, theft, slander, and intoxication remains happy.
A person who is not fanatical about goals, answers truthfully when asked, avoids petty quarrels, and does not get angry over lack of respect.
A person free from envy, compassionate, not resentful even when weak, not gossipy, and tolerant of differences is praised everywhere.
A person who is not arrogant, does not boast of heroism, is not haughty or abusive, remains always likable.
A person who does not revive settled enmities, is neither arrogant nor self-deprecating, does not angrily complain about misfortune, is praised as the best among the virtuous.
A virtuous person does not exult in own fortune, does not rejoice in others' suffering, does not regret or boast after giving.
A person who understands social hierarchy, follows local customs and caste duties, rises above others wherever they go.
A wise person abandons pride, delusion, envy, wickedness, hostility toward the king, slander, and public offense, and avoids conversation with drunkards, madmen, and wicked people.
A person who practices self-control, purity, devotion, auspicious rites, expiatory rites, and follows public opinion is favored by gods who elevate their status.

attributes.supernatural: Gods favor and elevate such a person
